label: AQ 0023
title: The org chart that merged too often

questions.q: If merging loses things, why not skip it and have a judge pick the best leaf?
questions.a: Because combining can add value. In Mixture-of-Agents (Wang et al., 2024), the aggregator beat an LLM ranker that picked one proposed answer, which suggests it was combining, not just selecting. So merge once, with every leaf in view.

teach.title: How it works: what the evidence says, and doesn't

questions.q: What if there are too many leaves for one synthesiser to read?
questions.a: Then some layering is unavoidable. Keep it wide rather than deep, as MacNet found wide shapes beat deep ones of the same density. Store each leaf's full output in files the synthesiser can open, as Anthropic's research system does to avoid a game of telephone. My suggestion: ask middle layers to list disagreements instead of rewriting.

teach.title: How it works: what the evidence says, and doesn't

questions.q: Who should do the one merge?
questions.a: Your strongest synthesiser, and test for it: by my reading, proposing and combining are different skills. In Mixture-of-Agents, WizardLM 8x22B reached a 63.8% AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate as a proposer but 52.9% as the aggregator.

questions.q: In the MacNet study, what makes a topology divergent or convergent, and which did better?
questions.a: Divergent nodes have more children than parents, so work spreads out; convergent nodes merge several inputs. With GPT-3.5, divergent versions of a star and a tree beat their reversed, convergent versions: 0.6267 against 0.5902, and 0.6015 against 0.5821.

teach.title: How it works: what the evidence says, and doesn't

questions.q: Why doesn't Mixture-of-Agents' success with layers of merging contradict the upside-down tree?
questions.a: Each Mixture-of-Agents agent reads every output from the previous layer, so no merger works from a slice. The org chart's problem is narrow merges stacked on each other, where the top sees only summaries.

teach.title: How it works: what the evidence says, and doesn't

questions.q: Each merge keeps a minority idea 80% of the time. How likely is it to survive three stacked merges, against one?
questions.a: About 51% (0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.512) against 80%, assuming each merge drops it independently.
